articles.title: Avengers: Doomsday Has a Bigger Challenge Than Bringing the X-Men Into the MCU
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Marvel Looking back, it seems like the most obvious thing in the world. After decades of successfully intertwining an entire universe of characters in Marvel Comics, it makes complete sense to at least try and bring that same scope and connective tissue to the big screen. But in 2008, Marvel Studios took a huge swing with […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Looking back, it seems like the most obvious thing in the world. After decades of successfully intertwining an entire universe of characters in Marvel Comics, it makes complete sense to at least try and bring that same scope and connective tissue to the big screen. But in 2008, Marvel Studios took a huge swing with Iron Man ’s post-credits scene . If it wasn’t well-received, then Marvel could have simply shrugged it off as a fun reference for hardcore fans. Instead, of course, Nick Fury’s mention of “the Avenger Initiative” gave birth to the Marvel Cinematic Universe and officially set the course for 2012’s The Avengers .

Bringing together Iron Man, Captain America, Thor, and The Hulk — all of whom previously led MCU films — into a crossover team film felt like a magic trick. And the fact that writer-director Joss Whedon effortlessly brought together these characters and their specific corners of the MCU undoubtedly lay the foundation that everything else is built on. Even more remarkably, the MCU has never stopped upping the ante. Throughout both the Infinity Saga and the Multiverse Saga, Marvel Studios has continually taken risks, but the biggest challenge in Avengers: Doomsday isn’t the one most people think it is.

The Avengers had to integrate heroes who, until that point, had occupied separate stories, each with its own unique genre and tone. However, Avengers: Doomsday has an exponentially more difficult task: combining several different teams . In hindsight, much of the Multiverse Saga seemed devoted to sprinkling in breadcrumbs that would gradually assemble a collection of superhero teams. Of course, Fantastic Four: First Steps and Thunderbolts* introduced fans to the Fantastic Four and the New Avengers , respectively. The latter team drew upon several different projects to bring its members into the MCU, especially Black Widow . And the Wakandans are already well established, most notably with Black Panther: Wakanda Forever .

But the past few years of Marvel projects have also been teasing the existence of at least two more teams. Avengers: Doomsday will finally see the MCU come face to face with Fox’s X-Men. Films like Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness and The Marvels featured cameos by popular X-Men characters , and Deadpool & Wolverine completed the mutants’ introduction. Meanwhile, X-Men ‘97 — while set in a different universe — reminded fans why they love these characters. But with more than two decades of films , the X-Men, their dynamic, and their powers hardly need an introduction to audiences. Rather, another team will have an uphill battle ahead in Avengers: Doomsday .

The last time the Avengers assembled was at the Battle of Earth. Following Tony Stark’s sacrifice, the team essentially disbanded. From a creative standpoint, this made sense for the MCU, as it would give the Multiverse Saga space to rebuild Earth’s Mightiest Heroes from the ground up. The trouble was that the Avengers still haven’t been rebuilt at all. In fact, the first mention of reassembling them was in Captain America: Brave New World , released just a year before Avengers: Doomsday . And yet, the new Avengers led by Sam Wilson’s Captain America — not the New Avengers led, it seems, by Florence Pugh’s Yelena Belova — will be central to this climactic chapter. In addition to Captain America, the team will reportedly include Thor (Chris Hemsworth), Ant-Man (Paul Rudd), Shang-Chi (Simu Liu), and Falcon (Danny Ramirez).

If this were a less complicated Avengers sequel, that team wouldn’t feel so rushed. But as Thor points out in the final Avengers: Doomsday trailer, he doesn’t even know who half of the heroes in the film are. With the exception of his relationship with Falcon, we don’t even know what Captain America’s leadership looks like. And this Avengers team is the only team in the film that doesn’t have even a single movie where they work together. It’s hard to imagine Avengers: Doomsday will have much of a chance to establish this new team dynamic before they rush into action due to all the whole universes colliding. With so much of a focus on expanding its hero roster, the Multiverse Saga forgot to connect all the dots within the Sacred Timeline , which would have only raised the stakes when other teams enter the fight.

Do you think the Multiverse Saga should have laid more groundwork to establish Captain America’s new Avengers team? Let us know in the comments section below!

Avengers: Doomsday arrives in theaters on December 18, 2026.

articles.title: ‘Outlander: Blood of My Blood' Bosses on the Season 2 Finale Twist That Would Rewrite the Series' Lore, Who Won't Appear on the Show — and Its Uncertain Future
articles.summary: SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers from “Twelfth Night,” the Season 2 finale of “Outlander: Blood of My Blood,” now streaming on Starz. “Outlander” was never a series to hold back on a brainy twist that took a minute to digest. But its prequel series, “Outlander: Blood of My Blood,” may have outdone its predecessor […]
articles.content:
SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers from “Twelfth Night,” the Season 2 finale of “ Outlander: Blood of My Blood ,” now streaming on Starz.

“Outlander” was never a series to hold back on a brainy twist that took a minute to digest. But its prequel series, “Outlander: Blood of My Blood,” may have outdone its predecessor with a twist that rewrites at least one family tree.

Since the prequel premiered last year, it has always operated on its own narrative timeline, separate from author Diana Gabaldon’s book series. In those books, Julia (Hermoine Corfield) and Henry (Jeremy Irvine), the parents of original series heroine Claire (Caitriona Balfe), died when she was 5 years old in a car crash. But with “Blood of My Blood,” executive producers Matthew B. Roberts and Maril Davis ponder what might have happened if they actually time-traveled through the same magic stones their daughter would decades later, and were left to survive in 1710s Scotland.

It has been one tragedy after another for the lovebirds, and that’s saying something, given that they weathered World War I. But one question has loomed large over the Beauchamps: What will happen to their son, William, with whom Julia was pregnant when they went through the stones? He’s not in Gabaldon’s books, so Roberts and Davis have a bit of freedom to play with his fate. And they seemingly gave fans their answer in the Season 2 finale.

Julia and Henry were dealt their biggest setback yet earlier this season, when a seer informed her she isn’t a time traveler, she was just pregnant with one. William has his father’s mystical gene, and now that Julia is postpartum, she won’t be able to go back to her own time unless they get pregnant again, which itself is a moral quandary. The news doesn’t stop them from trying to run away together again. But in the process, Henry is shot by Lord Lovat (Tony Curran) in a case of mistaken identity, and Julia’s attempts to flee Lovat’s henchman leave her lifeless at the bottom of a waterfall. Fearful for wee William’s life without his parents, Julia’s confidante Davina (Sarah Vickers) takes him to the safest place she can think of –– to her son Brian (Jamie Roy) and his new wife Ellen (Harriet Slater). Mere moments after Brian and Ellen’s long-awaited wedding, the Frasers have a new addition to their future home at Lallybroch. Related Stories Jennifer Lopez on the ‘JLo Show’ Concert Film, Her ‘Happy Era’ and Moving on From Divorce: 'What I Thought Love Was Really Isn’t Love’ ‘Morning Show’ Star Mark Duplass and Katie Aselton Show Off Their Three Rescue Dogs in PETA Ad (EXCLUSIVE)

This is where the series goes for broke, and makes a frankly brazen claim. Brian and Ellen are, of course, the parents of future “Outlander” hero Jamie (Sam Heughan). According to Gabaldon’s original books, he had an older brother named William (aka Willie), whose death when Jamie was young forever affected how he saw the world and cared for those he loved. (Not for nothing, Willie was so formative for Jamie that fans latched onto the wooden snake he carved before he died, and the onscreen prop sold for more than $5,000 at auction earlier this year.)

If “Blood of My Blood” is to be believed, Brian and Ellen being given an infant named William could mean that Claire’s heretofore unknown younger brother was actually raised as a Fraser 200 years in the past. It’s a twist that completely alters how fans should look –– at least in the TV series’ timeline –– at Claire and Jamie’s relationship. Not only does the prequel depict their parents as unexpected allies, but it is now suggesting they may have even shared a sibling, not by blood thankfully. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Now before anyone gets too excited (or angry!), Roberts and Davis aren’t exactly making this twist official on a birth certificate just yet: Even when pressed multiple times for confirmation, they dodged answering whether this really is the Willie of the Fraser family tree. But with Season 2 coming to a close without news about a Season 3 renewal, it’s hard not to feel the impact of this twist, given it could be the revelation the prequel leaves fans as a parting gift. For now, Davis is tying it all back to the original.

“With Willie/William, even if they're not the same person, I think it's so interesting to think how these two stories are interwoven now,” she tells Variety . “It binds Jamie and Claire's parents, and how will that affect them in the future? We always loved the idea that Jamie and Claire were meant to be, and we're seeing how that fate all comes together.” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Roberts has a bit more fun with his response about the mystery of it all. “I feel like this is the natural place to go, and I like to manipulate people,” he says with a grin. “That's my job.”

He isn’t kidding. Alternate endings were filmed for the finale, one where Ellen reveals to Brian that she is pregnant again right before they are handed William (an emotional beat, given that his father caused her miscarriage this season). So this could have been a case of two Williams. But Roberts suggests it was less of a possibility, and more of a security measure.

“I like to do some alt endings to throw people off in case scripts get leaked,” he says. “I like to keep actors on their toes, too. I have something in my head that I want to put on screen, but we did multiple endings with the finale of ‘Outlander’ as well.”

But rewriting lore to this degree is risky business, especially given the series isn’t yet guaranteed to come back. Still, Roberts and Davis have already planned out what would happen next should they get the go ahead, and there is one thing audiences won’t ever see in this prequel: young Jamie.

While diehard fans have undoubtedly done the math to figure out just how soon their favorite Highlander could make his debut, Roberts says he is hesitant to bring the action too close to the stories told in Gabaldon’s books and the original series.

“It's hard to think about the stories with young Jamie in them, because that feels like you're starting to tread on ‘Outlander,’ and I don't want to do that,” he says. “It feels like you want to get maybe as close to the birth of Jamie as we can, but that still gives us quite a bit of time.” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

If “Blood of My Blood” is at least in step with Gabaldon’s book series’ timeline, Willie is born in 1716 –– the same year of Brian and Ellen’s wedding, as seen in the Season 2 finale. Jamie will be born in 1721, so five years could be what’s left of the narrative runway for the series.

With those parameters in place, Roberts and Davis also continue to look beyond “Blood of My Blood” for future “Outlander” franchise opportunities. Even with the wealth of Gabaldon’s world building at their disposal (her 10th and final book has yet to be released), they continue to be vocal about a particular contender.

Lord John, a fan-favorite character played by David Berry in the original series, is the subject of Gabaldon’s companion series of novels, and Roberts and Davis previously tried to spin off those stories while the original “Outlander” was still airing. The series didn’t move forward then, but they seem to be actively hoping the franchise’s continued success will reignite interest.

“There are certainly other things out there for us to explore, and Lord John remains one of them,” Davis says.

articles.summary: A PS2 game is now available on PS5 and PS4 for $2.24, thanks to a new PlayStation Store sale that is live until December 1. Right now, the PS2 game in question is actually the cheapest PS2 game available on the PS Store, and unlike many PS2 games, which are included with a PS Plus […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google A PS2 game is now available on PS5 and PS4 for $2.24, thanks to a new PlayStation Store sale that is live until December 1. Right now, the PS2 game in question is actually the cheapest PS2 game available on the PS Store, and unlike many PS2 games, which are included with a PS Plus Premium subscription, this one is not. The only way to play it on PS5 or PS4 is to buy it, and it has never been cheaper than it is right now on digital Sony storefront.

As you may know, the underwhelming start of the PS3, combined with the historic success of the PS2, meant many PS2 games were released into the PS3 generation, and sometimes they skipped the newer Sony console entirely in favor of the older one. The King of Fighters '98 Ultimate Match from SNK Playmore is an example of this. The 2008 fighting game, a remake of the 1998 fighting game The King of Fighters '98 , was released on PS2 and in arcades two years into the PS3 lifecycle. And while it eventually came to Xbox 360, it didn't come to PS3.

The 2008 PS2 exclusive then came to PC in 2014, and then PS4 in 2022. This version was known as the " Final Edition ," and it most notably added online functions. Where the original game, The King of Fighters '98 , was considered one of the best fighting games of the late 1990s , the series never penetrated the mainstream market like fellow 90s fighting game series Tekken or Mortal Kombat , let alone 1980s Street Fighter . It was fairly niche in the late 1990s, was more niche by the time this remake came out in 2008, and is even more niche in 2026. That said, it's also very nostalgic for some PS2 users, and now it's some of the cheapest nostalgia on the PlayStation Store.

A Forgotten PS2 Fighting Game Those interested in the old-school fighting game may find it hard to jump into in 2026, not because it doesn't hold up. On the contrary, it holds up quite well. That said, it's a hardcore fighting game. For those with minimal experience with the series, it's not particularly newcomer friendly. At the very least, it has one of the steeper learning curves in the genre. Like just about any other fighting game series, it can enjoyed in a casual way easily. That said, without a story mode its offline content is not great. It's primarily an online game, which by and large rules out enjoying it casually.

If this PS2 nostalgia isn't to your liking, there is a first-person shooter PS2 series also currently on sale on the PlayStation Store for the same price . Meanwhile, an older 2001 PS2 classic is currently available for free for some users .

Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Avengers: Doomsday star Letitia Wright said that the future Black Panther will play a big role in the new Marvel Cinematic Universe movie. One of the biggest themes in Avengers: Doomsday surrounds the children of Marvel heroes and the idea that these characters are living stolen lives, while Doctor Doom lost his family. These Marvel children include the son of Steve Rogers and Peggy Carter , the adoptive daughter of Thor, and the son of the late King of Wakanda, T'Challa. When it comes to the latter character, he hasn't been shown in any of the trailers, but it seems that he will still play a role in the upcoming film.

In an interview with Entertainment Weekly about the upcoming MCU movie, Letitia Wright said that Shuri's main goal is to protect T'Challa's son, her nephew, as he prepares to take the throne. "Now that this threat of Doom is very near and close to her, she understands what is at stake for her own country," Wright said. "Not just the whole world, but for what they have going on in Wakanda. We have a future king that needs to be protected. Her brother's child, her nephew, and her country. So, that is a lot of weight on her shoulders. But from the cloth that Shuri is cut from, she's not afraid of that. She's gonna step right into it."

Shuri has more to protect now. pic.twitter.com/rLs0eFPAXr

While Wright talked about the importance of T'Challa II in the Avengers: Doomsday movie, don't expect him to play much of a role at all. The idea that Doctor Doom is coming for the children would likely just mean that Shuri knows she has to fight to protect her nephew back home, as well as the future of Wakanda. However, there is a very good chance that the child will play a major role in Avengers: Secret Wars next year. There are already rumors that the Young Avengers will have a big role in that movie, and the new Black Panther could fit in perfectly.

David Jonsson has been cast to play the new Black Panther , the son of T'Challa, and he will be in the next Black Panther movie, which will hit theaters in 2028. There is a great chance that he will show up as early as Avengers: Secret Wars . Remember that the character was introduced in Black Panther: Wakanda Forever in 2022, and he was very young at the time. Jonsson is much older than Divine Love Konadu-Sun was in that movie, so there are likely going to be some time-travel shenanigans to age him up to Jonsson's age by the time Black Panther 3 rolls around.

Avengers: Doomsday will have the main MCU heroes battling to save the world, and they will all fail in the movie. Avengers: Secret Wars could see the next generation of heroes fighting to recreate the world, and that could include T'Challa II and even an aged-up Franklin Richards, allowing them to succeed where their elders failed. However, for Avengers: Doomsday , just expect Shuri to fight with the other heroes to save Wakanda's future and her own nephew.

articles.title: The Supernatural Ending Jensen Ackles Actually Wants Is So Much Better Than What We Got
articles.summary: I would have wanted this instead.
articles.content:
Supernatural may have ended over six years ago, but the series is still a fan-favorite when it comes to rewatches with your Peacock subscription . The show’s 15 seasons were a roller coaster ride involving the Winchester brothers fighting just about everything Hell would throw at them, and more. However, Supernatural ’s controversial series finale has given fans a lot to talk about, and a lot of it is not great. After hearing Jensen Ackles ’ own version of the ending, I wish we had gotten that instead.

Ackles reiterated what the ending would have been had it not been for COVID while at a Supernatural fan convention ( via tvdkami) , and I am once again mourning what the pandemic took from us:

I would have loved more than anything for this to actually happen. The amount of characters that Supernatural introduced and killed off during its run, or just straight-up forgot about, was a large number. He went on to talk about Kansas performing, a moment that would have been absolutely perfect, given that “Carry On Wayward Son” was SPN ’s unofficial theme song. It would have looked like this:

Of course, there is only so much that could have been done at the time with all the restrictions, and at the very least, the series brought back Jim Beaver as Sam and Dean’s late surrogate father, Bobby Singer. That was better than nothing, in my opinion.

I would have been alright with an ending like this, despite it's shocking nature. Though I'll admit it's mostly because I wasn’t fond of how the finale turned out. Dean’s death dragged on, the penultimate felt more like a finale with how Sam, Dean and Jack defeated God/Chuck, and Castiel dying . Yes, things could and should have been different and they worked with what they had, but I still wish it had played out in a different manner.

articles.title: X-Files Creator Planning Reboot of His Other Cult '90s TV Series That Eventually Crossed Over
articles.summary: While discussions of ‘90s sci-fi television always led to The X-Files, its creator Chris Carter delivered not just that masterpiece but another as well. That would be the series Millennium which debuted in 1996 and got a criminally short three-season run but still managed a crossover with The X-Files. Now, it turns out that Carter […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google While discussions of ‘90s sci-fi television always led to The X-Files , its creator Chris Carter delivered not just that masterpiece but another as well. That would be the series Millennium which debuted in 1996 and got a criminally short three-season run but still managed a crossover with The X-Files . Now, it turns out that Carter is revisiting Millennium — and an actual reboot could be in the works.

Speaking with Film Stories , Carter revealed that he’s writing the first episode of a Millennium revival and while that episode writing is ongoing, he also suggested that there going be something bigger in the works for the cult-classic show.

“I was just sitting in a coffee shop working on the script, and I’m about halfway through, Carter said. “I’m hoping not just to make this pilot, because the timing is just right for it.”

Carter also noted that an executive is taking a look at the original 1996 Millennium pilot, which suggests that the work Carter is doing on a revival could indeed be for something much bigger.

Millennium never quite reached the same popularity as The X-Files and that’s a shame because the show was brilliant. The series followed Frank Black, an FBI profiler whose specialty was violent criminal — like, he was very good at getting into their heads, so much so that it made living a normal life a little challenging because he could genuinely see inside the mind of criminals, quite literally seeing through the eyes of killers. When we meet him, he’s left the FBI to join a private organization known as the Millennium Group. The series was unflinching and uncomfortable, and dark, even going so far as to suggest that Frank’s daughter, Jordan, had inherited her father’s abilities.

While the show was cancelled after just three seasons, it had something of a unique ending. Months after its final episode, it got a crossover of sorts with The X-File s in the seventh season episode aptly titled “Millennium.” It tied things up to an extent, but wasn’t a genuine conclusion to the series, though it makes for a good argument for timing of a Millennium return. As most fans know, The X-Files is getting a reboot from Ryan Coogler and while I’m not saying that the X-Files reboot would be connected to a Millennium revival, the fact that there is rich interest in The X-Files and the fact that Millennium inhabits a similar space makes a return to the latter series enticing. There’s also something to be said for the power of ‘90s nostalgia, which is strong right now, but perhaps even more important is how our culture has changed. There is something of an obsession with true crime now and while Millennium is something of a dark and twisted mirror of that — one can argue it even predicted the obsession — the interest in true crime now might finally give Millennium the audience it needs.

Would you want to see a Millennium revival? Let us know your thoughts in the comments.

articles.title: ‘Salvation’ Review: The Roots of Violence Are Explored in Emin Alper’s Tense, Atmospheric Study of a Massacre
articles.summary: How do you justify the unjustifiable? How do you get to the point where you feel morally in the right while you slaughter unarmed men, women and children? These are the questions director Emin Alper seeks to explore in "Salvation," a film notionally about the longtail fallout from a land dispute, but more elementally about […]
articles.content:
How do you justify the unjustifiable? How do you get to the point where you feel morally in the right while you slaughter unarmed men, women and children? These are the questions director Emin Alper seeks to explore in " Salvation ," a film notionally about the longtail fallout from a land dispute, but more elementally about how violence happens. Set in a Turkish village high in the mountains, the director's fifth film — and his first since the 2022's Cannes Un Certain Regard entry "Burning Days" — follows the trajectory of Mesut (an excellent and tragically believable Caner Cı̇ndoruk), whose personal insecurities set him on a path leading to a massacre. Mesut has always played second fiddle to his handsome younger brother, Sheikh Ferit (Feyyaz Duman). Their grandfather was an important man, seen by some as a savior of their village. He was their Sheikh, a local cultural and religious leader, and he passed this status on, not, as might have been expected, to the older brother, but to the younger. Meanwhile, Mesut’s wife is pregnant with twins and he is troubled by anxious dreams and thoughts concerning her sexual life. In the village, men mutter about their land being taken over by outsiders. Psychologically, then, Mesut is on the back foot. Sexual jealousy, sibling rivalry and a broader feeling of impotence in the face of potential threats from outside combine in a potent brew that, lacking the ear of a good therapist, isn’t going to turn out well for anyone. That’s not to say that Alper falls into the fallacy of laying everything that subsequently happens at one man’s door: On the contrary, this is a smart study of a community. Cı̇ndoruk gives a nimble performance as Mesut: At first, he plays a kind of low-status grudge-bearer, the sort of person who might be characterized as a boot-licker if there were any boots around that he deemed worthy of licking. Into this vacuum of leadership, as he perceives it, some chosen one must surely arrive. Lo and behold, he realizes it is he himself who must be reluctantly entrusted with the mission to protect his people. As he convinces others of his cause, he blossoms, and we see in his manner and bearing a man stretching himself out and becoming accustomed to power. One of "Salvation’s" greatest strengths is in capturing a subjective sense of the threat that the villagers collectively feel themselves to be facing. The signs, portents and omens come thick and fast, almost to the point of caricature: a burned field, uncanny storms, a sleepwalking child, a pair of identical twin girls herding goats, and theoretical religious discussions of the possibility of having confused the roles of Cain and Abel. The mood is one of permanent unease, with all the characters bubbling away together in a melting pot of distrust. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories ‘A Girl Unknown,’ ‘Crawling Into Myself,’ ‘Concrete Land’ Take Main Prizes at Doha Film Festival Monica Bellucci on Challenging Hollywood Ageism in James Bond, Working With Mel Gibson and the Power of Onscreen Nudity: ‘It’s Like a Costume That Brings a Role to Life’

Alper strategically avoids creating a clean delineation between dream worlds and reality. This deliberate decision to not formally telegraph dream sequences has an intentionally disorienting effect: We can't tell when a character is experiencing a dream or vision until something explicitly unreal takes place. While we might not sympathize with Mesut as he foments specific acts of violence, this all-pervading atmosphere of psychological threat helps us see how he convinces himself of his mission. This apposite demonstration of religious convictions being used to prop up concrete actions, spurred on and given fuel by tribalist rivalries, elevates "Salvation" from a merely striking mood piece to an astute psychological study. Sadly, the film isn’t mere fiction. In 2009, 44 people were murdered at a party in the Mardin Province of Turkey by masked assailants using automatic weapons and hand grenades. The attack left over 60 children orphaned. In taking this event as his starting point, Alper has created a film that is both culturally specific, and has plenty of wider applicability as well. There are, for instance, obvious parallels in "Salvation" with acts of violence committed by Israel in Gaza. But the relevance of "Salvation" is even broader: The rhetoric of politicians like Donald Trump or Vladimir Putin, or of U.K. Prime Minister Keir Starmer's statement that “we risk becoming an island of strangers,” plays on the same primal fears that allow Mesut to secure support for his bloodthirsty strongman tactics. As has been seen with ICE agents in the streets of Minneapolis, Mesut’s followers are very happy to indulge themselves in the sensation that they are noble soldiers defending themselves and their loved ones from foreigners, when they are in fact the aggressors. The fact that "Salvation" is not overtly and literally about ICE, Palestine or any of the aforementioned political figures may provide useful cover for any festivals, curators or distributors frustrated by institutional complicity or timidity in confronting these issues directly in their programming. This is simply a film inspired by a tragedy in rural Turkey that occurred nearly 20 years ago. And if audiences or critics wish to reach for contemporary parallels drawn from other examples of reprehensible violence? Why, then they may do so.

articles.title: Farhan Akhtar, Ashutosh Gowariker and Madhur Bhandarkar Look Back at 'Dil Chahta Hai,' 'Lagaan' and 'Chandni Bar' at 25
articles.summary: In 2001, three films challenged familiar conventions of Hindi-language cinema in very different ways. Farhan Akhtar's "Dil Chahta Hai" offered a new screen language for friendship and young adulthood; Ashutosh Gowariker's "Lagaan" turned a village cricket match into an epic about resistance; and Madhur Bhandarkar's "Chandni Bar" took audiences into the largely unseen world of […]
articles.content:
In 2001, three films challenged familiar conventions of Hindi-language cinema in very different ways.

Farhan Akhtar 's "Dil Chahta Hai" offered a new screen language for friendship and young adulthood; Ashutosh Gowariker 's " Lagaan " turned a village cricket match into an epic about resistance; and Madhur Bhandarkar's "Chandni Bar" took audiences into the largely unseen world of Mumbai's dance bars. Twenty-five years later, the filmmakers revisited the films and the risks behind them at "The Legendary 25s," a session at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa moderated by actor and producer Khushboo Sundar. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Chiwetel Ejiofor Was Afraid to Make ‘Backrooms’ Because of Director Kane Parsons’ Age: ‘He Was So Young!’ 'High Fidelity' Director Stephen Frears Still Teases Jack Black: 'I Told Him, You Owe All This to Me!'

One thread connected their stories: all three had encountered the expectations of commercial Hindi cinema before finding the conviction to make something different.

Gowariker and Bhandarkar already had films behind them before "Lagaan" and "Chandni Bar" established their identities as filmmakers. Akhtar, making his directorial debut with "Dil Chahta Hai," said he had not been interested in making a film that conformed to the prevailing Bollywood potboiler template.

For Gowariker, who is also the IFFI festival director this year, the turning point came after his first two films failed. Having initially tried to make commercial entertainers, he realized that "my next film had to be something I believe in, something that I want to make first, and then hope to God that the audience also likes it. So that's how the genesis of 'Lagaan' happened."

The idea was an unlikely proposition: a period drama built around a cricket match, with villagers taking on the British. Gowariker wanted to make a film about "a group of heroes." He researched the British Raj, 19th-century life, cricket and village communities before taking the script back to star Aamir Khan, who had initially rejected the premise. Gowariker asked Khan for just three hours to hear the narration of "Lagaan" before deciding. "He heard it. He laughed, he had tears and he said, 'I definitely want to do this now,'" Gowariker recalled of the film, which went on to receive an Oscar nomination. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Bhandarkar's route to "Chandni Bar" was rooted in observation. A visit to a dance bar with a friend gave him the subject for the Tabu-starring film, which he researched by visiting bars across Mumbai for six months. "Even if, in retrospect, 'Chandni Bar' had not done well at the box office, I would still be happy because this is the cinema which I wanted to make, and this is the world which I've seen," he said.

His interest in underdogs has continued in films such as "Page 3," "Corporate" and "Fashion," which examined the worlds of the media, business and fashion respectively. He has also resisted pressure to turn women-centered stories into male-led films for commercial reasons. From Tabu's vulnerable character in "Chandni Bar" to Raveena Tandon's politically ambitious woman in "Satta," he said he is drawn to complex women rather than idealized portrayals. "My movies are basically a mirror to society," he said.

With "Dil Chahta Hai," a buddy movie starring Aamir Khan, Saif Ali Khan and Akshaye Khanna, Akhtar set out to bring a more recognizable version of friendship to the screen. He felt Hindi films' depictions of male friendship did not reflect how people actually spent time together. "The relationship had become cheesy, filmy," he said. He cited Mansoor Khan's "Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak" (1988), which he watched as a schoolboy, as an important influence.

Asked specifically about the older-woman romance in "Dil Chahta Hai," he said the inspiration for the relationship between the characters played by Akshaye Khanna and Dimple Kapadia came "from many crushes that I had on older women, that's the honest truth."

The filmmakers also reflected on how cinema is made and judged. Akhtar described a screenplay as "a living, breathing thing," evolving through contributions from actors and crew members, sometimes well into the edit. Gowariker, discussing acting, said, "The true performance lies in the pauses where you're not saying anything."

On the industry's fixation with box-office numbers, Akhtar said, "Now the conversation is that I heard you had a great weekend. But I would rather know what you thought of the film." Gowariker described every new film as "a reset to zero," adding that the yardsticks had shifted over the years, from silver and golden jubilees to 100-day runs and opening weekends, making comparisons across films of different budgets and genres reductive. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Asked what they would change if they could revisit one another's films, Akhtar said he would leave "Lagaan" untouched, but if he were the producer, he would ask Gowariker to direct it again. Gowariker said he might add a soulful song to "Chandni Bar," while Bhandarkar said he would find it difficult to remake either "Lagaan" or "Dil Chahta Hai."

On AI and visual effects, Bhandarkar said, "AI and VFX can certainly enhance the visual experience and expand the possibilities of filmmaking, but they can never replace the human touch." Akhtar's advice to younger filmmakers was to draw on their own unique experiences.

articles.title: NBC Pulls Ad Criticizing U.S. Military Aid to Israel After Backlash, Reviews Approval Process
articles.summary: The ad aired during Wednesday's 'SNL' Thanksgiving special without senior NBC management's knowledge, a source familiar with the situation tells The Hollywood Reporter.
articles.content:
NBC will not air a controversial anti-Israel advertisement again after it drew backlash for airing during Wednesday night's Saturday Night Live Thanksgiving special.

A person familiar with the situation told The Hollywood Reporter that senior management was unaware of the advertisement until after it aired. NBCUniversal will now evaluate its advertising approval process to ensure appropriate levels of review.

The 30-second advertisement, titled "Every Three Seconds," shows a young girl saving money for a year by doing yard work, including mowing the lawn, blowing leaves and shoveling snow, until she raises $400 to buy a bicycle. The ad then cuts to a girl in Gaza, standing on crutches and missing a leg amid rubble, as the narrator draws a comparison between the two scenarios and U.S. military aid to Israel. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Business NBC Uses Thanksgiving TV to Kickstart 2028 LA Olympics Marketing Push TV Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade Postponed as Storm Descends on Northeast

"Over a year, she saved $400 for a new bicycle," the voiceover says. It then cuts to the girl in Gaza. "Every three seconds, our government sends $400 of taxpayer money to Israel to do this."

The advertisement was paid for by the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, or IMEU Policy Project. This pro-Palestinian advocacy nonprofit supports ending U.S. military aid to Israel. The group's campaign, titled "No More for Israel," encourages viewers to contact their congressional representatives to oppose continued military assistance to the country.

After the advertisement aired, several Jewish and pro-Israel organizations criticized NBC for broadcasting the spot.

Anti-Defamation League CEO Jonathan Greenblatt criticized the network in a post on X, writing , "Again and again, why do people in positions of authority fail to demonstrate basic decency, let alone respect, for the Jewish community? At a moment of escalating antisemitism, there is no rationale to justify fanning the flames with such a twisted narrative." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

B'nai B'rith International also condemned the advertisement in a Facebook post.

"Shame on NBC," the nonprofit wrote . "The suffering of innocent civilians is a tragedy. But using a child’s pain to spread a twisted, one-sided story that blames the Jewish state, and by extension Jews everywhere, is disgusting."

Jim Berk, CEO of the Simon Wiesenthal Center, also shared a statement with THR criticizing the network for airing the advertisement.

"The advertisement’s imagery, an American child’s hardship set against the anguish of a child in Gaza, offers viewers a seductive but unsubstantiated narrative: that the struggles of American families are somehow bound up with U.S. support for Israel," the statement reads in part. "In collapsing a complex foreign policy into a single, emotionally charged imagery, erases the deeper realities, including the imperative to protect Israeli lives and the very existence of the country itself. By manipulating emotion and stripping it of context, this ad seeks to become a catalyst for hostility."

Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping has certainly defied its own title, as the film ate heartily at the box office during the Thanksgiving holiday. The box office tally is now in, and reports have Sunrise on the Reaping earning $11.6 million at the box office on Thursday, followed by Focker-in-Law ($7.7 million), the latest installment of the Meet the Parents franchise starring Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro (with Ariana Grande joining the cast), and Disney's animated movie Hexed, which earned $4.5 million.

Right now, box office projections have Sunrise on the Reaping earning $85 million over the entire Thanksgiving holiday weekend, which would bring its domestic total up to over $230 million and set a new competitive milestone for the franchise.

Sunrise on the Reaping is the second Hunger Games prequel film, following The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes , which was released in 2023. That film was only a moderate success, earning $363 million worldwide ($166.3 million domestically), while receiving mixed reviews from critics. It was enough for Lionsgate to once again partner with author Suzanne Collins when she planned her follow-up book, Sunrise on the Reaping . Now the second prequel film will earn more at the domestic box office in one week than Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes did during its entire theatrical run.

While some may be surprised by the amount of box office dominance happening here , no one should be surprised that Sunrise on the Reaping is performing better than The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes . This latest installment of The Hunger Games is much more directly connected to the original film franchise, as it follows Haymitch Abernathy (Katniss Everdeen's mentor, played by Woody Harrelson) and his hellish experience in the 50th Hunger Games, aka the 2nd Quarter Quell.

There are several legacy characters recast with popular actors, while younger actors like lead actor Joseph Zada and co-star McKenna Grace are quickly becoming breakout stars. All in all, Sunrise on the Reaping is helping to create a much bigger Hunger Games saga that spans between the events of Sunrise on the Reaping and The Hunger Games: Catching Fire , when Haymitch and other revolutionaries finally make their move and start the Rebellion during the 75th Hunger Games (the 3rd Quarter Quell).

Meanwhile, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes had the unenviable task of telling an origin story for The Hunger Games franchise villain, President Coriolanus Snow (Tom Blyth), and the seeds of his hatred for District 12 and Katniss Everdeen – a concept that put some fans off the moment Suzanne Collins announced the book. The film adaptation proved to be equally challenging for a lot of die-hard fans and mainstream viewers alike, as The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes turned out to be much more of a character drama than the action-thriller experience that the best Hunger Games films offer.

To his credit, director Francis Lawrence (who has directed every Hunger Games film after the first installment) has weathered the highs ( Catching Fire ) and lows ( Mockingjay ) to reach this point where The Hunger Games franchise feels like a complete, cohesive, and sweeping cinematic saga. And Sunrise on the Reaping drives that point home beautifully and poetically by the end .

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is now in theaters.

It's been a rough year for Star Trek , as the 60th anniversary gave fans more heartache than happiness. We lost two big stars in Patrick Stewart and Walter Koenig, Skydance canceled Starfleet Academy , and now we're learning the company also axed Michael Dorn's chances to return as Worf.

It's extra interesting considering that Terry Matalas recently revealed what his plan was for Star Trek: Legacy , and the Klingons played a big part in it . Was the franchise quietly working on a spinoff that would bring the Picard showrunner back into the fold?

That news isn't too surprising, as it's clear at this point Skydance isn't worried about rushing the next phase of Star Trek programming. The company's primary concern is to get the franchise back in theaters, and a script is already in development with hopes it'll achieve that goal.

articles.title: Predicting Awards Season’s First Big Week: Who Wins at the Gothams, NYFCC, NBR and More
articles.summary: The starting gun of the Oscar season starts Monday, and by next Sunday, it will have a shape that many of us will be able to see clearly. For months, the Oscar race has run on festival premieres, studio screenings and ever more elaborate predictions, mine included. This week, the people with ballots finally speak. […]
articles.content:
The Gothams have long been a launching pad for independent cinema, a place for films that might otherwise get flattened by the studio machine. In 2023, the organization scrapped its $35 million budget ceiling and opened more categories to international titles. The result is a more eclectic ballot, one that puts established auteurs and first-time filmmakers side by side. This year, that means 42 features and 25 performances across 11 categories.

That makes the Gothams a natural first stop for “The Invite,” which we expect to win best feature. Wilde’s ensemble piece, starring Seth Rogen, Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton, has the kind of dinner-party-argument appeal that plays well with this voting body. “Josephine” is my alternate and could follow some jaw-dropping selections like “A Different Man” two years ago. The drama took both the U.S. Grand Jury Prize and the Audience Award at Sundance in January, and the Gothams have never lost their appetite for championing a discovery.

Notably, a different set of industry professionals, five jury members each, for each category, pick the Gotham winners, while Gotham members vote on the audience award. A film can win a jury on artistic grounds while another finds its people in the wider membership.

Best Feature: “The Invite” (A24) Alternate: “Josephine” (Sumerian Pictures)

Director: Ryusuke Hamaguchi, “All of a Sudden” (Neon) Alternate: Mike Leigh, “Tender Loving Care” (Bleecker Street)

Lead Performance: Andrew Scott, “Elsinore” (Focus Features) Alternate: John Malkovich, “Wild Horse Nine” (Searchlight Pictures)

Supporting Performance: Tao Okamoto, “All of a Sudden” (Neon) Alternate: Kate O’Flynn, “Tender Loving Care” (Bleecker Street)

Breakthrough Performer: Guitarricadelafuente, “La Bola Negra” (Netflix) Alternate: Adia, “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” (Amazon MGM Studios)

Audience Award: “You Can See Everything” (A24) Alternate: “La Bola Negra” (Netflix)

Breakthrough Director: Jordan Firstman, “Club Kid” (A24) Alternate: Aleshea Harris, “Is God Is” (Amazon MGM Studios)

Original Screenplay: “Tender Loving Care” (Bleecker Street) — Mike Leigh Alternate: “Wild Horse Nine” (Searchlight Pictures) — Martin McDonagh

Adapted Screenplay: “The Invite” (A24) — Rashida Jones and Will McCormack Alternate: “Minotaur” (Mubi) — Simon Lyashenko and Andrey Zvyagintsev

Documentary Feature: “Naza” (The Guardian, MK2 and Neon) Alternate: “You Can See Everything” (A24)

International Feature: “Possible Love” (Netflix) Alternate: “Blue Heron” (Janus Films)

Founded in 1935, the New York Film Critics Circle is the country’s oldest film critics organization and one of the most influential early stops on the calendar. Its history is full of choices that challenged the Academy’s conventional wisdom. Many of them went on to become landmarks, even when they diverged from the eventual Oscar winner.

This year, we’re predicting “You Can See Everything” to show its strength by winning the top prize for best film, with “The Odyssey” as the alternate. Fielder and Oppenheim’s 174-minute portrait of Elizabeth Holmes premiered as Telluride’s secret screening and has drawn the kind of critical fervor usually reserved for narrative features. A best film win from New York wouldn’t automatically make it an Oscar best picture contender, but it would move the film into a different tier of consideration. “The Odyssey” is the more traditional choice: a major filmmaker, a sweeping production and a likely force in the technical categories.

In directing, Wilde could pull off a deserved citation ahead of Nolan, who has never won from the group before.

Andrew Scott is my choice for actor, with Robert Pattinson’s combined work in “Primetime” and “The Drama” as the alternate. Julianne Moore could win actress for “The Debut,” with Sandra Hüller for “Rose” as a real threat. In supporting actor, Guitarricadelafuente could keep building momentum for “La Bola Negra,” with a surprise citation for someone like John Cho of “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” (much like Regina Hall or Tiffany Haddish surprised in their respective years). Kate O’Flynn (“Tender Loving Care”) and Amanda Seyfried (“You Can See Everything”) could be in a battle for supporting actress, or someone else completely.

The screenplay prize could go to Jordan Firstman for “Club Kid,” with Cristian Mungiu’s “Fjord” as the alternate. “Tangles” is my animated film pick over Laika’s “Wildwood,” an interesting split between independent animation and a more established studio shop.

Best Film: “You Can See Everything” (A24) Alternate: “The Odyssey” (Universal Pictures)

Director: Olivia Wilde, “The Invite” (A24) Alternate: Christopher Nolan, “The Odyssey” (Universal Pictures)

Actor: Andrew Scott, “Elsinore” (Focus Features) Alternate: Robert Pattinson, “Primetime” and “The Drama” (A24)

Actress: Julianne Moore, “The Debut” (A24) Alternate: Sandra Hüller, “Rose” (Mubi)

Supporting Actor: Guitarricadelafuente, “La Bola Negra” (Netflix) Alternate: John Cho, “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” (Amazon MGM Studios)

Supporting Actress: Kate O’Flynn, “Tender Loving Care” (Bleecker Street) Alternate: Amanda Seyfried, “You Can See Everything” (A24)

Screenplay: “Club Kid” (A24) — Jordan Firstman Alternate: “Fjord” (Neon) — Cristian Mungiu

Animated Film: “Tangles” (Independent Film Company) Alternate: “Wildwood” (Laika)

Cinematography: “Project Hail Mary” (Amazon MGM Studios) — Greig Fraser Alternate: “La Bola Negra” (Netflix) — Gris Jordana

Nonfiction Film: “Rehearsals for a Revolution” (Sony Pictures Classics) Alternate: “Naza” (The Guardian, MK2 and Neon)

First Film: “Club Kid” (A24) — Jordan Firstman Alternate: “Obsession” (Focus Features) — Curry Barker

Founded in 1909, the National Board of Review has named a Top 10 every year since 1929. Unlike the critics’ groups, it’s made up of New York-area film enthusiasts rather than working critics. Its selections land just as studios are deciding which campaigns deserve more fuel, which makes it one of the earliest industry signals of the season.

Variety is predicting “Project Hail Mary” for best film, with “Artificial” as the alternate. That would be a fitting choice for a group that has long rewarded accessible, ambitious filmmaking. Phil Lord and Christopher Miller could also take director, ahead of Denis Villeneuve for “Dune: Part Three.” That would follow the three-year current trend of the same film winning both prizes.

If both happen, “Project Hail Mary” has an instant entry for best picture.

The acting picks could be just as revealing, but they don’t always match up with Oscars, so you have to consciously pick an acting winner that probably won’t translate (i.e., Elle Fanning in “A Complete Unknown” or Will Forte in “Nebraska”). Seth Rogen is my actor prediction for “The Invite,” with Matt Damon for “The Odyssey” as the alternate. Inde Navarrette could win actress for “Obsession,” although she can win breakthrough performer. Rachel Zegler won best actress for “West Side Story” (2021) instead of breakthrough her respective year.

John Leguizamo could follow veteran winners who tend to win supporting actor with “The Odyssey.” A "no guts-no glory" pick exists with Elizabeth Debicki could taking supporting actress for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” with Samantha Morton for “The Odyssey” projected as the runner-up.

The screenplay categories offer openings for two very different films. James Gray could win original screenplay for “Paper Tiger,” ahead of Curry Barker for “Obsession.” In adapted, Sian Heder and Rebekah Taussig could be recognized for “Being Heumann,” with “La Bola Negra” as the alternate.

The specialty awards could be telling, too. I’m predicting “Wildwood” for animated feature, Anthony Ippolito for breakthrough performance in “I Play Rocky” and Barker for directorial debut with “Obsession.” “La Bola Negra” could win international film, while “You Can See Everything” is my documentary pick. Hoyte van Hoytema could take cinematography for “The Odyssey,” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” could win stunt artistry. “Naza” is my choice for the NBR Freedom of Expression Award.

The lists may matter as much as the prizes. For the Top 10, look for glaring omissions but don’t put too much stock in them. “The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King” (2003) settled for the NBR’s ensemble prize without a Top 10 slot, and Guillermo del Toro’s “The Shape of Water” (2017) was left off entirely. Both won best picture. The NBR’s lists are an early endorsement, not a verdict.

Best Film: “Project Hail Mary” (Amazon MGM Studios) Alternate: “Artificial” (Neon)

Director: Phil Lord and Christopher Miller, “Project Hail Mary” (Amazon MGM Studios) Alternate: Denis Villeneuve, “Dune: Part Three” (Warner Bros.)

Actor: Seth Rogen, “The Invite” (A24) Alternate: Matt Damon, “The Odyssey” (Universal Pictures)

Actress: Inde Navarrette, “Obsession” (Focus Features) Alternate: Julianne Moore, “The Debut” (A24)

Supporting Actor: John Leguizamo, “The Odyssey” (Universal Pictures) Alternate: Adam Driver, “Paper Tiger” (Neon)

Supporting Actress: Elizabeth Debicki, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” (Netflix) Alternate: Samantha Morton, “The Odyssey” (Universal Pictures)

Original Screenplay: “Paper Tiger” (Neon) — James Gray Alternate: “Obsession” (Focus Features) — Curry Barker

Adapted Screenplay: “Being Heumann” (Apple Original Films) — Sian Heder and Rebekah Taussig Alternate: “La Bola Negra” (Netflix) — Javier Ambrossi, Javier Calvo and Alberto Conejero

Animated Feature: “Wildwood” (Laika) Alternate: “Toy Story 5” (Pixar)

Breakthrough Performance: Anthony Ippolito, “I Play Rocky” (Amazon MGM Studios) Alternate: Jaafar Jackson, “Michael” (Lionsgate)

Directorial Debut: Curry Barker, “Obsession” (Focus Features) Alternate: Lance Oppenheim, “Primetime” (A24)

International Film: “La Bola Negra” (Netflix) Alternate: “Fjord” (Neon)

Documentary: “You Can See Everything” (A24) Alternate: “History of Concrete” (Magnolia Pictures)

Cinematography: “The Odyssey” (Universal Pictures) — Hoyte van Hoytema Alternate: “Digger” (Warner Bros.) — Emmanuel Lubezki

Stunt Artistry: “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” (Sony Pictures) Alternate: “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” (Sony Pictures)

NBR Freedom of Expression Award: “Naza” (The Guardian, MK2 and Neon) Alternate: “Elsinore” (Focus Features)

The American Film Institute’s annual selections live in a different space from the critics’ prizes. There are no individual performances and no craft citations, just 10 films the institute considers culturally and artistically representative of the year. The Top 10 is restricted to American productions. Works that fall outside its criteria can receive an AFI Special Award, as Kenneth Branagh’s “Belfast” and Questlove’s documentary “Summer of Soul” did in 2021 and Jafar Panahi’s “It Was Just an Accident” did last year.

That makes the AFI list a measure of which films have entered the industry’s broader conversation. There’s no single winner, and because the list is alphabetical, it isn’t a ranking.

We’re thinking: “Artificial,” “Dune: Part Three,” “Elsinore,” “I Play Rocky,” “The Invite,” “Michael,” “The Odyssey,” “Project Hail Mary,” “Wild Horse Nine” and “Wildwood.” “Obsession” is my alternate.

“You Can See Everything” is my Special Award prediction, with “La Bola Negra” as the alternative since neither can win.

Alternate: “Obsession” (Focus Features)

AFI Special Award: “You Can See Everything” (A24) Alternate: “La Bola Negra” (Netflix)

Founded in 1975 by critics working in print, radio and television, LAFCA has become one of the most respected critics' groups in the country. It votes and announces in December, then presents its awards at a ceremony in January.

We’re seeing “The Odyssey” for best film, with “You Can See Everything” as the alternate. That would hand Nolan a major critical endorsement in a week when New York may have gone the other way. That's exactly why the opening stretch matters: different groups can watch the same year of movies and come away with very different pictures.

For director, I'm going with Andrey Zvyagintsev for “Minotaur,” ahead of Ryusuke Hamaguchi for “All of a Sudden.”

With non-gendered acting categories, the group chooses two lead and two supporting performances.

Lead performance could produce one of the more distinctive outcomes of the season, with Jeon Do-yeon for “Possible Love” and John Malkovich for “Wild Horse Nine” sharing the prize. Virginie Efira for “All of a Sudden” and Andrew Scott for “Elsinore” are the alternatives.

In supporting performance, Andrew Garfield could win for “Artificial” alongside Amanda Seyfried for “You Can See Everything.” Penélope Cruz for “The Invite” and Anne Hathaway for “The Odyssey” are the alternate selections.

The screenplay award could go to Jones and McCormack for “The Invite,” with Firstman's “Club Kid” as the alternative. Add it up: a Gotham best feature, a possible New York director win and an LAFCA screenplay prize would give “The Invite” a broad critical footprint before the guilds have said a word.

On the craft side, I'm predicting Linus Sandgren for cinematography for “Dune: Part Three,” Adam Locke-Norton for editing for “You Can See Everything” and Ludwig Göransson for music score for “The Odyssey.” “Backrooms” could surprise in production design, with Danny Vermette ahead of Donald Graham Burt for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”

If “You Can See Everything” wins both editing and documentary, pay attention. A documentary competing in a category usually owned by narrative films would strengthen the argument that it belongs in the larger best picture discussion.

Best Film: “The Odyssey” (Universal Pictures) Alternate: “You Can See Everything” (A24)

Director: Andrey Zvyagintsev, “Minotaur” (Mubi) Alternate: Ryusuke Hamaguchi, “All of a Sudden” (Neon)

Lead Performance: Jeon Do-yeon, “Possible Love” (Netflix) and John Malkovich, “Wild Horse Nine” (Searchlight Pictures) Alternates: Virginie Efira, “All of a Sudden” (Neon) and Andrew Scott, “Elsinore” (Focus Features)

Supporting Performance: Andrew Garfield, “Artificial” (Neon) and Amanda Seyfried, “You Can See Everything” (A24) Alternates: Penélope Cruz, “The Invite” (A24) and Anne Hathaway, “The Odyssey” (Universal Pictures)

Screenplay: “The Invite” (A24) – Rashida Jones and Will McCormack Alternate: “Club Kid” (A24) – Jordan Firstman

Cinematography: “Dune: Part Three” (Warner Bros.) – Linus Sandgren Alternate: “Primetime” and “You Can See Everything” (A24) – David Bolen

Editing: “You Can See Everything” (A24) – Adam Locke-Norton Alternate: “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” (Amazon MGM Studios) – Cam McLauchlin

Music Score: “The Odyssey” (Universal Pictures) – Ludwig Göransson Alternate: “Behemoth!” (Searchlight Pictures) – The Behemoth! Collective

Production Design: “Backrooms” (A24) – Danny Vermette Alternate: “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” (Netflix) – Donald Graham Burt

Foreign Language Film: “All of a Sudden” (Neon) Alternate: “Minotaur” (Mubi)

Documentary/Nonfiction Film: “You Can See Everything” (A24) Alternate: “Naza” (The Guardian, MK2 and Neon)

Animation: “Iron Boy” (Sony Pictures Classics) Alternate: “Hoppers” (Pixar)

New Generation: Curry Barker, “Obsession” (Focus Features) Alternate: Jordan Firstman, “Club Kid” (A24)

Douglas Edwards Experimental Film Award: “Naza” (The Guardian, MK2 and Neon) Alternate: “Everybody to Kenmure Street” (Icarus Films)

articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Darkseid created the Absolute DC Universe to strip away the good and make evil more pronounced. He took away advantages that some heroes had, such as Superman's earthly family, Wonder Woman being raised on Themyscira, and Batman having wealth to finance his superhero career. However, he also made the villains even more terrifying. In the Absolute Superman comics, that version of Brainiac is scarier than any version the Man of Steel has ever had to face. When looking at the Absolute Batman villains, they are even more terrifying, and some border on extreme nightmare fuel.

Scott Snyder and Nick Dragotta didn't just give Batman's rogues' gallery new costumes in Absolute Batman , but they turned the villains into body-horror monsters that make the original villains look absolutely tame in comparison. Every villain compares in some way to its original depictions, but all of them are infinitely scarier, and one of them is pure nightmare fuel.

Absolute Mr. Freeze debuted in Absolute Batman #7 (2025) by Scott Snyder and Marcos Martin. In the main DC universe, the character debuted as Mr. Zero in Batman #121 (1958) by Dave Wood, Sheldon Moldoff, and Bob Kane. He became Mr. Freeze in the comics in Detective Comics #373 (1968) after the 1966 Batman TV series used the name. He then received a sympathetic backstory thanks to Batman: The Animated Series in the 1990s.

The Absolute version is a completely different person. This is Victor Fries Jr., the son of scientists Victor and Nora Fries, who froze him as a child, and the freezing mutated him. He was horrifying, with icy blue skin, dark veins, and a hunched, unnatural way of moving. He runs V-Core, turns unwitting volunteers into ice zombies, can freeze anything he touches, and keeps his own frozen parents in search of a cure. He also works for the Joker and is in no way the sympathetic Mr. Freeze from the main Batman comics.

Absolute Clayface debuted in Absolute Batman #22 (2026) by Scott Snyder and Werther Dell'Edera. He made his full debut one issue later, and this is where he proved to be one of Batman's deadliest threats. The original Clayface, Basil Karlo, debuted in Detective Comics #40 (1940) by Bill Finger and Bob Kane as a B-list actor with no superpowers who wore a clay mask and killed people in the order their characters die in a film. It wasn't until Matt Hagen in Detective Comics #298 (1961) that he became a shape-shifter.

In the Absolute Universe , Basil Karlo is an Ark M experiment created by the Joker. He shifts between liquid mud and hardened clay, and puddles of his mud follow him like shadows. Anyone who steps in that mud delivers their template to him so he can become them. In Absolute Batman #23, he changed form to look like Batman and killed Tim Drake, making it look like Batman was now a cold-blooded murderer. The main look is a mixture of John Carpenter's The Thing and a being from House of Wax .

Batman is a monstrous human being compared to the main DC Batman, and Bane is even bigger than that. Absolute Bane first appears in Absolute Batman #9 (2025) by Scott Snyder and Nick Dragotta. The classic Bane debuted in Batman: Vengeance of Bane #1 (1992) by Chuck Dixon and Graham Nolan, and this led into the "Knightfall" storyline where Bane became an immediate threat when he broke Batman's back. The version in the Absolute DC Universe makes the original version of Bane look like nothing.

His origin is similar, but the difference is that Absolute Bane kills his own revolutionary father to accept the offer to work for the Joker. He stands about nine feet tall without Venom and can swell to the size of a small building with it. Absolute Bane broke Batman with little effort in Absolute Batman #9 before guarding Bruce in Ark M for months in the next issue. Venom also gives him precise control over his muscle cells and lets him expand his brain to hold more knowledge, so he is a strategist as well as a giant.

Scarecrow is a different kind of frightening in Absolute Batman , and instead of looking like a terrifying monster, he is a lot more cerebral and terrifying because of his more eerie appearance. Absolute Scarecrow debuted in Absolute Batman #19 (2026) by Scott Snyder and Nick Dragotta. The classic Scarecrow debuted in World's Finest Comics #3 (1941) by Bill Finger and Sheldon Moldoff, and his fear toxin never debuted until years later, when he was reintroduced in 1966.

In the Absolute Universe, Dr. Jonathan Crane is one of Ark M's most terrifying doctors, and the Joker recruits him to work for him. His origins were a mystery, as a flock of crows always follows him. He goes barefoot, his eyes and mouth are stitched shut, his speech balloons have uneven lines, and he carries a cigarette that may deliver his fear toxin. He has used his fear toxin to kill Jim Gordon and Joe Chill, both with Batman watching. The fact that Scarecrow does not look like a monster but still delivers terrifying moments speaks volumes.

Out of all the Absolute Batman villains, the Joker is the definition of nightmare fuel. The Absolute Joker first appeared briefly at the end of Absolute Batman #1 (2024) by Scott Snyder and Nick Dragotta, as a wealthy, normal-looking man with slicked-back hair who killed people who joked around him. His monster form and origin arrived in Absolute Batman #15 (2025). The classic Joker debuted in Batman #1 (1940) as a criminal, and he has changed a lot over the years. However, he has never been as terrifying as he is in Absolute Batman .

Joker's name is Joseph "Jack" Grimm V , but the Jack Grimm I-V family line is one man posing as several generations. He was a Gotham orphan who, in 1888, used laughing gas to drug the local crowds and rob them. In monster form, he stands about 15 feet tall with green horns, long claws, and rows of teeth, and #15 is the first time readers hear his laugh. He hunts and eats people on a private island, drains the blood of orphans in his charities to stay young, and funds several villains. When he and Batman finally fought, Batman never stood a chance.

Who are your favorite Absolute Batman villains? Let us know who you think is the most terrifying in the comments below.

articles.title: 5 Twisted Romance Anime That Will Break Your Heart
articles.summary: While some of the most popular romance anime that stay at the top of watchlists are fluffy, low-stakes slice-of-life romps, there is a large subsection of anime fans looking for something a little darker than the average love story. Whether it be character tropes like the infamous yandere archetype, with the timeline-hopping obsessive girlfriend Yuno […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google While some of the most popular romance anime that stay at the top of watchlists are fluffy, low-stakes slice-of-life romps, there is a large subsection of anime fans looking for something a little darker than the average love story. Whether it be character tropes like the infamous yandere archetype, with the timeline-hopping obsessive girlfriend Yuno Gasai from Future Diary that dominated the 2010s to rival yakuza families getting tangled into messy love affairs or even doomed soulmates whose bond goes beyond the grave, dark romance anime have gradually become more sought after every single year.

One of the most important components of these doomed romance stories, however, is their capacity to break fans' hearts. Whether it be through bittersweet reconciliation that allows the leading couple to stay together, or, in more tragic cases, end up separated despite being soulmates. There are plenty of anime who try and achieve a balance of impeccably written romance with twisted, dark themes, but very few manage to achieve it in a way that both resonates and sticks with audiences after the final episode.

Scum's Wish is an incredibly unique spin on twisted romance, as the series doesn't take its audience through steamy red light districts or introduce ravenous supernatural partners, instead, the series takes place in a very normal high school, with seemingly very normal teenagers. Utilizing the "fake dating" trope, the anime follows Hanabi Yasuraoka and Mugi Awaya as they enter a falsified relationship to emotionally cope with their feelings for other people.

Scum's Wish presents itself with contrasting color palettes and character designs much better suited for a typical slice-of-life romance that dives into some of the darker, more cynical feelings that can emerge from unrequited love; as the story progresses, the characters must combat their own self worth, grapple with intense feelings of co-dependency, and struggle with choices that don't always boil down to black and white solutions. The 12-episode anime is available on Prime Video.

A cult-classic that unfortunately flew under the radar when it originally released, Devils' Line follows a university student in her early twenties named Tsukasa Taira, a relatively normal young woman who becomes entangled, and eventually enraptured, with a half-vampire named Yuuki Anzai who works in a police task force in Tokyo tasked with hunting vampires plaguing the city. In Devils' Line , the form of vampirism in-universe doesn't require that the vampire drink blood to sustain themselves, instead, experiencing strong emotions can trigger an insatiable bloodlust and need for violence.

The anime's leading couple meet for the first time when Tsukasa learns about the existence of vampires when a longtime friend reveals his true nature and attempts to kill her. She has an unlikely encounter with Anzai, who saves her life, with the two becoming entangled as Anzai acts as her protector going forward. Given Devils' Line 's exploration into supernatural romance with a creature whose emotional regulation constantly puts Tsukasa's safety in question while obsessively acting as her protector, it's no surprise the anime has become a hit with fans of darker romance stories. Depending on region, Devils' Line can be streamed on Netflix, with the physical Blu-ray release available through online retailers.

Based on a dating sim of the same name, Diabolik Lovers is an infamous reverse harem series that places a soft-spoken human girl into a den of vampires who grow absolutely obsessed with her. Yui Komori is sent to live in a secluded mansion with six handsome and sadistic brothers who treat her as their own "sacrificial bride" and feed off her as often as they can without outright killing her. The 24-episode anime series dives into all the twisted romance narrative threads that make the genre so famous, exploring deep-rooted obsession, the effects of generational trauma, and fears of abandonment that morph into a tragic love story.

The overarching story follows Yui as she learns more about her own history and abilities as a human capable of seeing and comprehending supernatural phenomena. Considering Diabolik Lovers is based on a dating sim, the anime is relatively vague on who Yui will end up with, creating the perfect battleground for shipping wars among fans. Unfortunately, Diabolik Lovers isn't available on any major streaming platforms, however, the anime has been collected into different DVD and Blu-ray collections that can be purchased through online retailers.

Yakuza Fiancé , based on the steamy josei manga of the same title , follows Yoshino Somei, a no-nonsense heiress and granddaughter of Osaka's most prolific yakuza boss who is arranged to marry Kirishima Miyama, the grandson of a syndicate leader from Tokyo in an effort to unite the two rival families. Behind Kirishima's charming persona, the young man hides a disturbed and manipulative streak that causes him to make reckless decisions and respond to conflict in an extremely volatile manner. Yoshino, unable to stand down and be a submissive bride pushes back on his awful attitude, creating an ongoing power struggle between the couple.

The 12-episode anime beautifully depicts the mind games employed by both Kirishima and Yoshino to try and get the upper hand on the other, and the longer they pretend to despise and wish ill will on the other, the more it becomes apparent that they're absolutely obsessed with one another. Aside from exploring the main pair's romance, the series also explores many of the intricate issues plaguing areas under yakuza control, showing the negative effects of rival factions and the consequences of battling over territory. Yakuza Fiancé is currently available to stream on Crunchyroll for audiences around the world.

A major breakout hit for dark and twisted romance fans in 2026, Firefly Wedding has all the makings of a series in the genre that also interweaves the heartache of inevitable tragedy. Set in the Meiji-era, Firefly Wedding follows Satoko Kirigaya, a noblewoman with a debilitating heart condition destined to cut her life short. Wishing to wed and make her family proud of her before the inevitable comes, Satoko is abducted and nearly killed before striking a deal with one of the assassins to marry him in exchange for his protection.

Shinpei Gotou, the assassin, is an eccentric, ruthless, and stunningly handsome man who becomes smitten with Satoko right away, whisking her away to "protect" her, despite her circumstances. Satoko is a beautiful young woman who knows how to play into her feminine nature to win over the mean around her, and as she and Shinpei toy with each other's feelings to make the other jealous, Shinpei's devotion to Satoko takes the pair down an obsessive spiral of unprecedented romance.

As of writing, the series is still currently airing and is slated to conclude its first season with 12-episodes. The anime currently available to stream on Crunchyroll. What kind of romances do you like to watch the most? Let us know your thoughts about it in the comments.
