Seventeen-year-old Leah Sava Jeffries carries the weight of the world on her shoulders in Season 3 of "Percy Jackson and the Olympians" — literally. The story […]
articles.content:
SPOILER ALERT: The following story contains plot details from "I Learn How to Grow Zombies," Season 3, Episode 3 of “ Percy Jackson and the Olympians ,” now streaming on Disney+.

Seventeen-year-old Leah Sava Jeffries carries the weight of the world on her shoulders in Season 3 of "Percy Jackson and the Olympians" — literally. The story of Atlas, a Titan burdened by the unbearable task of holding up the sky, is one of the many Greek myths that serves as the basis for a Season 3 storyline. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Doha Film Festival Showcases Five Projects From Qatar's Industry as Local Filmmakers Hail Start of a 'Golden Era' Producer of Oscar-Nominated ‘A Friend Of Dorothy’ to Make Directorial Debut With Disability Drama ‘Hidden Creatures,’ Easyjet Founder Boards as EP (EXCLUSIVE)

The Season 3 premiere saw Jeffries' Annabeth kidnapped by a human-lion-scorpion hybrid monster called a manticore and taken across the country from Percy ( Walker Scobell ) and Grover (Aryan Simhadri). Annabeth faces her own struggles while her friends work to rescue her, which is new for the show; the first two seasons followed the trio going on epic quests together. With Annabeth separated for much of "The Titan's Curse" — the third book in Rick Riordan's "Percy Jackson" series, which Season 3 is based on — Jeffries' main scene partners now are Charlie Bushnell, who plays Luke, and Dafne Keen, who plays Artemis.

That's not the only way Season 3 is wading into uncharted waters. The first-ever screen interpretation of "Percy Jackson" was a pair of movies in the early 2010s based on Riordan's first and second books. But Jeffries is keenly aware of the fact that "The Titan's Curse" has never been adapted.

“It's the first time anyone has ever seen it live action instead of just reading it in the book,” she says. “I want to make sure that I'm still delivering how the description was as much as I can, but then also still giving my own little twist with it.” While dedicated readers of the "Percy Jackson" books love to see Easter eggs in the TV show, Jeffries never wants the show to be for those fans alone. She points out many viewers hadn't read the books until Seasons 1 and 2 came out and aims to perform for that audience too — especially as someone who hadn't even been born yet when the original novel was released in 2005, she points out. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"Coming into these roles in the beginning was a tough thing because [the books] had such a big fan base already, and so many people that already knew about them before me," Jeffries says. "It was a lot to learn from, but I'm so excited that I was able to get this role and embody the character as much as I can."

Jeffries says she has learned a lot from Bushnell, 22, whom she acted opposite in several key scenes in Episodes 2 and 3 this season. She recalls him checking in after fight scenes or making sure he didn't accidentally hit her during a take.

"He's such a role model for people. I learned so much stuff from him. He's just such a great person to work with as well as a scene partner," Jeffries says. "You could just tell he loves doing what he does, and that's such a big thing to see because even before the show has come out, with criticism, sometimes I still get in my head. But when I watch him working, his confidence and the way he goes about things, it just makes me have a brighter day, so I'm very grateful to work with him."

In Episode 2, Annabeth discovers that Luke has been subjected to the punishment that once burdened. Atlas, the Greek Titan: holding up the sky. She decides to takes over him, and when the weight hits her shoulders, she lets out a guttural yell that Jeffries says was hard to find — and sounds different than she remembers. "The crazy thing is that it sounds so much more high-pitched on the show. I promise you, I have videos when I had a deeper scream and it was grittier, but I think I just lost my voice at that time," she says, adding that the outburst didn't come naturally to her: "I'm not a screaming person. Someone can ask me right now. like, 'Hey, scream!' I cannot just open my mouth and be like, ' Ahhh !' Like, I can't."

So Jeffries devised a trick. If she needs to scream on camera, she pushes against something or strengthens her core with a quick sit-up beforehand. "I will growl before, and then go," she says. "I have to know that my voice will hit it."

In the show, when a character is carrying the weight of the sky, an eerie, gray haze spreads across their eyes — achieved with color contacts. That visual detail was actually Jeffries' idea. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

She says she told Daphne Olive, one of the "Percy Jackson" writers, that using contacts would give more weight to the scene. “The grayness puts the strain on your eyes. It shows that you're in this different world and this different dreaming life,” Jeffries says. Eventually, Jeffries got approval from the production to move forward with her pitch.

In Episode 3, still stuck in the gray haze, Annabeth has a vision of herself holding onto Percy and Thalia (Tamara Smart) as they dangle over a cliff. It's an emotional sequence — Annabeth has tears in her eyes — but Jeffries mostly recalls how awkward it was to film. On set, she was hanging off of a practically built cliff and was fitted with wires, "because obviously, they don't want me to fall," she says. And though Jeffries had Percy and Thalia on her mind, she didn't have Scobell and Smart to look at. "Whenever you saw my face, they actually weren't even there, and I wasn't talking to them," she says. "I was actually holding two weights while hanging over the top, which is the funniest thing ever. Everyone was staring at me. When I looked down — I always try to do my best, but — I was so nervous."

At the suggestion of her acting coach, Jeffries took some quiet time to concentrate before her more emotional scenes. "It was hard because I love making jokes," she says, "but the scene came out so beautifully. I just loved it."

Percy and Annabeth don't share many moments together during Season 3, with the former going on a lengthy journey to rescue the latter. But Jeffries and Scobell spent a lot of time working together on Seasons 1 and 2, so when thinking about how to develop their relationship this season, Jeffries says they just went for it.

"It's crazy because we really didn't [talk], but in a good way," she says. "I like the fact that we had our own assumptions of what it would be like, and then just see how we were going to play it on the actual day."

For their scenes together, the pair would just follow their instincts without a discussion for a few takes, then put their heads together to see what else they could build. "We just knew that if we were to leave it to ourselves, then it would be better when they say action," Jeffries adds. "We were going to learn from there."

From Jeffries' perspective, the best is yet to come. She says she's especially excited to see her work with Bushnell in Episode 5 — "The improv we did was genuinely crazy," she says — and teases that a big surprise is coming in the Season 3 finale. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The last episode "is something that literally means so much to me because I feel like so many people have asked for it," she says. "I know so many people who wanted to see it, and that dream came true."

articles.summary: It’s been 18 years since Hancock opened in theaters, with the Will Smith-starring superhero movie offering audiences a bit of a fresh take on the genre with Smith’s Superman-esque character having some serious flaws and his story some surprising turns. A sequel has long been teased, but now, director Peter Berg just gave the biggest […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google It’s been 18 years since Hancock opened in theaters, with the Will Smith-starring superhero movie offering audiences a bit of a fresh take on the genre with Smith’s Superman-esque character having some serious flaws and his story some surprising turns. A sequel has long been teased , but now, director Peter Berg just gave the biggest update yet on that project — and not only is it one that sounds promising, but Smith himself is on board to return if they can get the universe to “line up”.

Speaking with Variety , Berg said that Smith has sent him a script for Hancock 2 and that not only is the script great, but he is also very on board to make it. Berg also said that, should the sequel end up happening, it would be a very special film.

“I don’t even know if I’m supposed to say it or not, but Will sent me an incredibly funny, great script for Hancock 2 ,” Berg said. “I would do it. The Universe has to line up.”

“I think the time is right for Will to do that role , and for many reasons,” he added. “I think Will Smith is a really good human being and a very, very talented human being and just like me and I would guess you, not a flawless human being. I’m flawed. I’ve made some mistakes, and I’ll probably make some more. But I love Will Smith, and I always will. And I know a lot of other people do, too. So, if this ever happens, it would be, I think, a really special film.”

Berg’s comments about it being the right time for Smith to do the Hancock sequel is interesting and it actually makes a great deal of sense if you step back and look at Smith’s professional life. As many people will recall, there was the incident at the 2022 Academy Awards where Smith slapped Chris Rock on stage. This led to Smith receiving a decade-long ban from Academy events and certainly impacted his reputation and perception with audiences. Given that the plot of the first Hancock movie involved a bitter anti-hero whose reputation with the public was soured by the property and personal damage created by his heroic attempts and saw Hancock redeem himself.

While Smith isn’t necessarily having to win people over after property damage in the furtherance of superheroing, the idea of picking up the story of a character working to redeem himself would go a long way in reminding audiences who he is beyond that infamous Oscars moment. More than that, Hancock was a very successful and popular movie. The film made $629.4 million at the box office on a budget of $150 million and landed as the fourth-highest grossing film of 2008. It’s a film that people genuinely enjoyed and wanted more of — it frequently is noted by fans that the film made for a great first chapter of a trilogy at the time. There’s something to be said about making your comeback not only a story well-suited to the situation, but one that brings back a much-loved character and continues his story as well.

Now it’s your turn to weigh in: do you want that Hancock sequel? Let us know your thoughts in the comments or hit us up on the forum.

In wake of this, a high enhanctress Uchawi and a small group of rebels rise from the shadows with the power of forbidden magic to defy his absolute power.

articles.title: Rick Moranis Reveals He Secretly Directed Scenes From an '80s Cult Classic
articles.summary: Rick Moranis added an uncredited directing gig to his incredible run of movies in the 1980s. Forty years after the release of Little Shop of Horrors, the actor has revealed that he spent some time behind the camera on the musical horror comedy. Director Frank Oz had recently welcomed a child and wanted to spend […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Rick Moranis added an uncredited directing gig to his incredible run of movies in the 1980s. Forty years after the release of Little Shop of Horrors , the actor has revealed that he spent some time behind the camera on the musical horror comedy. Director Frank Oz had recently welcomed a child and wanted to spend some time with his family. Unfortunately, the technically ambitious production was already running behind schedule. Moranis stepped in for Oz, inadvertently making the director look bad in the process.

In a rare interview with Empire celebrating the movie's 40th anniversary, Moranis explained that he had the luxury of shooting material that didn't involve the movie's famously elaborate man-eating plant. Oz was regularly spending entire days on just a handful of camera setups because of the technical demands of bringing Audrey II to life. Without having to contend with the enormous puppet, Moranis was able to get through considerably more material. The actor managed to get through between 12 and 14 setups while filling in for the director. Apparently, Oz still gives Moranis a hard time about how productive he was during his brief stint directing the movie. Directing wasn't the only skill Moranis had to put to use on Little Shop of Horrors . While the actor was already an accomplished comedic performer, he was determined to do his own singing in the adaptation of Howard Ashman and Alan Menken's stage musical.

Few directors in Hollywood were better equipped to tackle the technical challenges of Little Shop of Horrors than Oz. The longtime collaborator of Jim Henson had already co-directed The Dark Crystal , directed The Muppets Take Manhattan , and brought Yoda to life in two Star Wars movies. Even with his considerable experience as a puppeteer, getting Audrey II to convincingly perform musical numbers proved to be a challenge.

The larger versions of Audrey II couldn't move fast enough to keep up with the vocals provided by the Four Tops' Levi Stubbs. Oz compensated by filming the puppet at a lower frame rate, allowing its movements to be sped up when the footage was projected at a standard frame rate. Unfortunately for Moranis, that meant the actor had to sing and move in slow motion whenever he shared the frame with Audrey II during those musical numbers. Even something as simple as walking required Moranis to rethink how he was using his body.

The production would face an entirely different challenge when test audiences rejected the movie's original ending . Oz had remained relatively faithful to the stage musical, which saw Seymour and Audrey, Ellen Greene, meet their demise before Audrey II and its offspring took over the world. Audiences had grown so attached to Moranis and Greene over the course of the movie that they weren't particularly receptive to watching the pair get eaten. Oz ultimately gave audiences the happy ending they wanted, though fans can now watch the movie with its original ending restored.

Oz would reunite with Moranis just four years later for My Blue Heaven , a comedy that afforded the director the luxury of working with Moranis and Steve Martin without having to accommodate an enormous puppet. As much as Oz might still give Moranis grief about his productivity behind the camera on Little Shop of Horrors , he clearly enjoyed having him in front of it. Audiences will finally get to see Moranis back on the big screen in 2027 when he reprises his role as Dark Helmet in Spaceballs 2 . articles.title: 'The Hunting Wives' Stars and Creator Break Down Margo and Sophie's Dangerous Love Affair in Season 2: 'It's a F—-ed Up Commitment' to 'Move Past' Murder
articles.summary: SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for Season 2 of "The Hunting Wives," now streaming on Netflix. Earlier this month, Texas shocked the nation by electing Democrats to the governorship, the U.S. Senate and several more key positions during this year's midterm elections. But the Lone Star State's politics have always been seen as dynamic […]
articles.content:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for Season 2 of " The Hunting Wives ," now streaming on Netflix.

Earlier this month, Texas shocked the nation by electing Democrats to the governorship, the U.S. Senate and several more key positions during this year's midterm elections. But the Lone Star State's politics have always been seen as dynamic and complicated to those in the know — like fans of "The Hunting Wives," Netflix's juicy, campy drama series about a group of wealthy, gun-loving and sexually fluid women from East Texas.

"I love our show, because you see both sides of this coin, and we're making fun of each side," says "The Hunting Wives" star Brittany Snow about the series' depiction of Texas politics. Co-star Malin Åkerman adds, " We're not going to say that we had anything to do with it, but there's all these different people saying, 'The Hunting Wives' had something to do with Texas going blue!' It's a fun little moment for us right now."

Åkerman plays Margo Banks, the housewives' confident ringleader whose Republican husband Jed (Dermot Mulroney) is a favorite to become governor. But, in Season 1, her beautiful house of cards is torn apart with the arrival of Sophie (Snow), an East Coast liberal who is shocked by the dirty underbelly of her new Southern home. Margo is full of secrets that she's intent on keeping from Sophie, and thinks she's in the clear when the two begin falling in love (and deep, deep lust). But Season 1 ended with Sophie discovering that Margo had gotten pregnant by a teenager, Brad (George Ferrier), before having an abortion and murdering Brad's girlfriend, Abby Jackson (Madison Wolfe), for uncovering the truth. The only saving grace for Margo is that Sophie can't do anything with the information, because when her brother, Kyle (Michael Aaron Milligan), attempts to intimidate Sophie on Margo's behalf, Sophie hits him with her car and kills him instantly. Now, they're both in trouble.

Because Sophie hid Kyle's body and told no one what she did, Season 2 begins with Margo trying to get back into her good graces. Unaware that Kyle is even dead, she keeps calling his number, getting no response until a panicked Sophie uses AI to deepfake Kyle's voice and keep the illusion up. In person, Sophie tries her best to avoid Margo, but she can't control herself. So she uses Kyle's voice to ask Margo whether any of their relationship was genuine. When Margo answers that it was "100% real," not just a ploy to cover-up the murder, Sophie is finally ready to get back together. She meets Margo at the Banks' lake house, where they have sex — which is rudely interrupted by Zelda (Dale Dickey), a woman from Margo's past, who sneaks up and holds a gun point-blank to Margo's head.

Zelda is the leader of a biker gang in Alba, Margo's hometown. She suspects Kyle of impregnating and murdering her underage granddaughter, Ellie (Chloe Guidry), and is attacking Margo to get information about Kyle's whereabouts. Zelda and the gang don't believe Margo when she says she has no idea where he is until Sophie blurts out that Kyle couldn't have killed Ellie because she killed him. Zelda pieces together that it was someone in the gang (Cam Gigandet as Gentle John) and shoots him in the head. Soon, the police show up and the gang gets shot to death. Margo and Sophie are escorted home before they can discuss what happened, and Sophie panics, worrying that Margo will tell the police what happened to Kyle. But she doesn't. After ignoring several calls from Sophie, Margo shows up at Sophie's apartment and forgives her — they're even, since Margo is a murderer too. Related Stories Producer of Oscar-Nominated ‘A Friend Of Dorothy’ to Make Directorial Debut With Disability Drama ‘Hidden Creatures,’ Easyjet Founder Boards as EP (EXCLUSIVE) 'Ramayana' Doubled Visitors at Kerala's Jatayu Rock, Official Says as India Pitches Itself to Global Productions at WAVES Film Bazaar

The two begin secretly dating again, but Jed and his staff keep Margo on a tight leash during his campaign for governor. So Sophie hatches up a plan: If Margo publicly admits that she's had an abortion, she'll be able to tank Jed's campaign and leave him for Sophie while drumming up enough support and attention to maintain her wealthy lifestyle. Snow: The car scene in the rain was a really difficult scene because there had to be so many things at once happening. The push-pull of a toxic relationship: "Please stay in my car. I love you. I also need you to get out. Also, I killed your brother. Also, I'm gonna have a nervous breakdown." And it's all those levels while looking really, really terrible on my part. Like a drowned rat.

Åkerman : I loved that that was the first scene where we see them together, because there was so much going on and there are high stakes. Hopefully people feel the same way, like, "Oh my god! Just stay! Kiss! Get together!"

Snow: It was a good scene. That kinetic energy that we have. The anger that I have. You trying to win me over. It's a lot!

Åkerman : I mean, Margo comes first. She's always gonna have her own back. But I truly think that somewhere deep inside, this is the closest to a feeling of love that Margo has had for anyone. There's something about Sophie that really draws her in, and she feels the most herself that she's ever felt. There's some version of true love, as well as her survival. She can't turn that off yet because it's not safe yet to turn it off, and she has to make sure that she's not going to get called out. So there's a big duality there.

Rebecca Cutter: It was reverse engineering to get Sophie and Margo back together. The biker gang is looking for Kyle, and [since he isn't available], who can Margo go to when she's threatened? Sophie's the only one that knows she killed Abby. Sophie's the only one that knows the real her. So having that threat come into her life, in the form of Zelda and the gang, sends her directly to Sophie. Then Sophie, having to interact with Margo through the AI deepfake, falls in love with her all over again and feels guilty about what she's done. It was this perfect storm bringing them back together. The other thing of that makes their reunion possible is that Sophie has grown and changed a lot over the two seasons. Åkerman : You just never know how it's gonna be edited together. But shooting it was it was a lot, over the course of two or three days. A lot of emotion. Snow: The juxtaposition of the show is really encapsulated in that scene. The comedy, the drama, the thriller.

Snow: I hate that scene. Because you really see how desperate Sophie is in that moment. I don't know if any more veins in my neck and forehead could have popped out. She's desperate, and she doesn't know if Margo's going to forgive her, so the fact that she does is pretty crazy.

Åkerman : I loved that scene. You're brilliant in it. All the veins. I love it all. I love it all.

Åkerman : It's a lot, and but I do think that Sophie is the closest thing to family that she has after her brother. Snow: We have this in common now.

Åkerman : I do think it was a lot to process. But she almost wins that cat-and-mouse chase, because she goes, "Well, now I'm back on top. I get to pull the strings and call the shots." Cutter: Margo is, above all else, a survivor and a schemer. In a very practical sense, she recognizes that Sophie has something on her, with Abby Jackson, and she has something on Sophie, with Kyle. It's like Russia and the United States. It's a cold war. But now we're even, so it's a great place for them to be.

Snow: Murder brought us together!

Snow: Sophie's coming from such a nervous breakdown that any forgiveness feels like such an oasis in her mind, and especially because it comes from Margo. There's hope in that scene. When you see Kyle's dead body [get discovered], you realize hope is never going to last long on "Hunting Wives." Åkerman : I don't know if I'd say the purest. Afterwards, I think it gets purer. But in that moment, Margo holds onto a few other things other than loving intentions. Snow: Our physicality in that scene is interesting, because you're sitting there the whole time just watching me, and I'm pacing around, doing a tap dance. You're just like, "Dance, monkey."

Cutter: It was important to show that the relationship is more than just sex, and that there is this deeper commitment that they're making to each other to move past this, even though it's kind of a fucked up commitment. So she's wrestling with the decision to, maybe for the first time in her life, choose herself. And that feels really good to her. Åkerman : I may not have a great answer for you. I think it's more about the suspense, because we want to believe she's about to say this, and to give it that really great twist at the end. Snow: But don't you think she's taking her power back? Like, "You can't cage me, Jed. I'm still gonna say what I want."

Åkerman : I guess you're right. Thank you for that!

Cutter: It's partly to mislead the audience, also because Sophie said something to her on the phone call earlier: "You could be a hero to half the country." Snow: Trying to cover up another murder, which always brings them together. I mean, we leave off this season with a cliffhanger, where it's open to the audience whether Sophie feels like she might hear Margo's voice or maybe she doesn't. And Margo's covered in blood, so we get to see these women in totally different places, physically and mentally, and they're on a level that makes them feel like equal adversaries in a lot of ways. Snow: I think she's going to own herself.

Åkerman : We're gonna have to watch.

Snow: We're gonna watch, and we're gonna like it!

Cutter: I don't watch that much reality TV, but I think I would have to try it. Imitation is the sincerest form of flattery.

articles.summary: Can we make this a franchise, please?
articles.content:
With Hallmark’s upcoming movie , Holiday Ever After: A Disney World Wish Come True, set to premiere on the 2026 Christmas movie schedule , it’s hard not to think about a possible sequel for this Disney World-set movie. Considering it took place in Florida, it only feels natural that it could expand to more Disney Parks around the world. So, I asked the cast, director and a producer where they want to go next for another Hallmark romance, and I’m obsessed with their answers.

Despite feeling like vampires while filming at Disney World at night, the cast of Holiday Ever After: A Disney World Wish Come True had a blast working and living in the parks . So, they were all thrilled when I brought up the idea of doing another one in a new location. For director Ryan Landels, Tokyo is the dream, as he explained:

As he said that, Richard Kind, who plays Alan, jumped in to ask why DisneySea differs from the other parks. In response, Landels explained that it takes some inspiration from “Jules Verne,” and he noted that there are rides there he’d “never seen” before.

Again, I think this would get my vote too. As someone who has only been to the parks in the United States, I think it'd be so fun to live vicariously through these characters as they head to DisneySea. Seconding that, Richard Kind excitedly said:

Christy Carlson Romano, who was sitting between the two men and plays Nicole in the movie, also said “sign me up” in regard to that idea. Bryce Durfee, who plays Sam, also said “let’s go to Tokyo” during my interview with him, Kiera actress Taegen Burns and producer David Wulf. However, while he name-dropped Tokyo (and Paris) as well, there’s a different location he discussed with Durfee and Burns that I think is worthy of (another) movie too.

While the cast and creatives named a few great places Holiday Ever After could go next, there’s also something to be said for staying in Disney World. To that point, producer David Wulf told me:

He makes a fair point: Disney World is a massive place, and they could easily make a sequel there. To that point, I asked them which rides they’d like to highlight if they were to keep the Holiday Ever After magic in Florida. Here’s what they had to say:

Well, there’s certainly more magic to see at Disney World. However, I’m also hoping that Holiday Ever After’s team finds themselves in Japan too. Really, I’ll be happy with a movie at any of the Disney Parks. However, these ideas the cast and creatives threw my way are phenomenal.

Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Brad Bird's filmography has some of the greatest classic and modern animated features on it ( The Iron Giant, The Incredibles, Ratatouille, The Incredibles 2 ), and he's trying to add another hit with his upcoming Netflix film, Ray Gunn . A mix of classic Film Noir and futuristic sci-fi, Ray Gunn stars Sam Rockwell as the voice of Raymond "Ray" Gunn a cop turned private detective. Ray gets plunged into a case involving a murder, an alien plot, and a potential femme fatale in the form of his love interest Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson), a prominent star of the screen.

ComicBook.com's Chris Killian had the chance to sit down with Brad Bird at the press junket for Ray Gunn . With so many big family-friendly animated movies under his belt, Ray Gunn feels slightly more adult with its Noir tropes and themes. So would Brad Bird be willing to take it a step further and do a full-fledged R-Rated animated film?

In his own words, Brad Bird does have some idea about the R-rated animated film he would make, and the one condition for him agreeing to do it: "It would have to be story driven, but I've made that argument before that, you know, there are films," Bird said.

"Some people think of animation as a rating, almost like it's a G or PG rating. And if it's anything other than that, then it's not, you know, what animation does. And I don't think of it that way, he continued. "I think of a film like The Godfather, it's rated R, and I wouldn't change a frame of it. But I also wouldn't have my kids see it at ten; I would probably wait 'til they're like 13, 14, you know what I mean?"

With that kind of outlook, it's all about timing for Bird – and now is not the current time for him to make the move to a more restrictive-rating for his animated projects. "I don't see myself at this point doing that because I don't have an idea that is suitable for that. But, I would love to make every kind of film, you know, and I certainly would not say no to an R-rated film if it was the right R-rated film."

Ray Gunn is set "In Metropia, a gigantic city in an alternate future as seen from 1939," where we meet "private eye Raymond Gunn (Sam Rockwell)" who gets "drawn into a case involving aliens, murder and a multimedia star named Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson)." Additional cast members include Tom Waits as Ray's alien partner Eye-ra Kadok, with Matt Berry ( What We Do In The Shadows ), Bobby Cannavale ( Man on Fire ), Michelle Rodriguez ( Fast X ), Alan Tudyk ( Creature Commandos ), Michael Chernus ( Severance ), Patton Oswalt ( Agents of SHIELD ), and others.

Brad Bird's Ray Gunn will get a limited release in select theaters starting on December 4th. It will start streaming on Netflix on December 18th.

Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google It's hard to think of a more iconic toy duo than Kenner and Star Wars . The manufacturer got the rights on the toy line immediately after the release of the first movie, and boy did it make sure to leverage it. From the early bird mail-ins and the original 12 figures to the massive AT-ATs and detailed starships, Kenner captured almost each and every facet of the original trilogy, including the most Glup Shitto of characters. Many of the earlier toys are now worth thousands and even millions of dollars, making them the most prized possessions in the toy collector community. However, every now and then, someone manages to nab one of them for a an absolute steal, like this fan's Tatooine Skiff .

Over on Reddit, a fan posted their latest thrift store find, and it's one of the best looking Kenner Tatooine Skiffs I've seen in a while. Now here's the kicker: while this Star Wars vehicle goes for anywhere between $800 - $1,200, depending on its condition, this fan managed to get theirs for just $8.49. That's a bigger steal than Andor's payroll heist on Aldhani. What makes this even more impressive is that the Skiff is in great condition, with all rails and supports in place. Some collectors consider the Tatooine Skiff to be the rarest Kenner Star Wars vehicle on the market, which means this fan just managed to nab a Holy Grail for almost nothing. It's clear that the thrift shop had no idea what they had in their hands.

Some people just have all the luck in the world, and it looks like Redditor nostalgiast99 might have been on top of the lucky list that day. Managing to find this Grail in such a good condition is nothing short of having the Force on your side. Sure, it would have been even more impressive if it was still in the box, but this find is well worth $900 to $1,000 on its own. However, in cases like these, it's not the monetary value that matters, it's the sheer endorphin rush you get from finding the item. And, in case that rush wasn't enough, it's doubled by the fact that they got it for an absolute bargain. I mean, at this point the thrift shop might as well be paying them to take it.

It's unclear whether the figures in the image are from the shop or belong to the collector, but if it's the latter, the find is even more special since they already had most of the related figures. The comments section is filled with people who can scarcely believe this find. One comment asked if they also found a $20 bill on their way into the store, as it's one of the luckiest find they have come across. Another comment can't believe that this unsealed Tatooine Skiff is still in such a good condition. The rest of the comments either congratulate the collector on the find or convey their jealousy. This is one of those supremely rare instances where the stars align to make the find rare, well preserved, and at a massive discount. It's almost akin to finding a Khyber crystal.

What's your greatest ever thrift store toy find? Let us know in the comments!
